title: Archon — Interview and Demo Preparation
purpose: Practice concise, credible explanations without overstating implementation evidence.
limitations: This is derivative learning material, not canonical implementation evidence.
Demo scripts and interview answers must be revalidated against the source commit before use.
A polished explanation, screenshot, or recorded artifact never upgrades local evidence to public deployment or production readiness.

concepts.label: Product Thesis
concepts.summary: Archon is an evidence-first local Agent Reliability Workbench built around governed execution and inspectable runs.

teaching.definition: The product thesis is the shortest accurate statement of the problem Archon solves and the boundary in which it has been proven.
teaching.responsibility: Frame Archon as a control plane for policy, approvals, tools, evidence, and evaluation rather than as a generic chatbot or public platform.
teaching.failure_behavior: If the opening overclaims deployment or hides the control-plane purpose, later evidence cannot repair the audience's mental model cleanly.
teaching.why_it_matters: Interviewers evaluate judgment as much as feature count; a precise thesis establishes credibility immediately.

concepts.boundary: The workbench is local and portfolio-oriented; it has no public production endpoint or traffic evidence.
concepts.narration: Open with the problem and boundary: Archon is a local Agent Reliability Workbench that governs and inspects agent runs. It is not a public production service or a chat wrapper claim.
concepts.scenario: An interviewer asks, What is Archon, in one sentence?
options: A production AI platform used at scale
A local reliability workbench for governed, inspectable agent runs
concepts.scenario_explanation: The answer states product purpose and evidence boundary without hype.

concepts.label: Architecture Spine
concepts.summary: Policy → Run → Approval → Tool → Evidence → Evaluation is the stable narrative spine.

teaching.definition: The architecture spine is a compact ordering of responsibilities that lets a presenter trace authority and evidence without listing every subsystem.
teaching.responsibility: Connect model intent to deterministic authorization, bounded execution, durable records, and later quality judgment.
produces: A diagram the audience can retain
controls: The model proposes but does not authorize
teaching.failure_behavior: Skipping policy or evidence turns the story into a generic model/tool loop; merging evaluation into runtime obscures proof timing.
teaching.why_it_matters: A stable spine keeps two-, fifteen-, and forty-five-minute explanations consistent while depth changes.

concepts.boundary: The spine is a teaching abstraction; not every optional proof path executes on every request.
concepts.narration: Use one memorable spine: policy, run, approval, tool, evidence, evaluation. Then explain that the model proposes while deterministic code owns authority, limits, persistence, and execution.
concepts.scenario: A presenter says every run always performs RAG, verifier delegation, and recorded evaluation inline.
options: Correct that optional proof paths are separate and differently timed
concepts.scenario_explanation: The architecture explicitly separates optional grounding, verifier, and post-run evaluation paths.

concepts.label: Claim Ladder
concepts.summary: Exists, wired, tested, observed, UI, live-provider, and deployed must be assessed independently.

teaching.definition: The claim ladder is an evidence discipline that prevents one artifact from being stretched across dimensions it did not prove.
receives: Observation, UI, provider, and deployment evidence
teaching.responsibility: Name the strongest supported dimension and retain every weaker or missing dimension explicitly.
controls: A mock is not live evidence
teaching.failure_behavior: Missing evidence yields unproven or partial status, never an inferred green check.
teaching.why_it_matters: Credible engineering communication depends on stating exactly what was exercised and what remains unknown.

concepts.boundary: Passing deterministic tests establishes contracts, not learning efficacy, public operation, or broad provider quality.
concepts.narration: Use the claim ladder for every major statement. Code existence, wiring, tests, observation, UI, live provider, and deployment are independent. Never promote one dimension by implication.
concepts.scenario: A Kubernetes manifest is present but has never been applied.
concepts.scenario_explanation: A manifest is not a deployment observation.

concepts.label: Code and Test Proof
concepts.summary: Exact symbols and behavior tests make architecture claims inspectable and reproducible.

teaching.definition: Code proof ties a spoken claim to the implementation seam that owns it and to a test asserting the external behavior or invariant.
teaching.responsibility: Show where the contract lives, how dependencies are wired, and which failure path the test would catch.
controls: Tests describe behavior rather than screenshots
teaching.failure_behavior: A stale symbol, test double, or implementation-detail assertion cannot support a current product claim without rechecking the path.
teaching.why_it_matters: Specific anchors let an interviewer challenge design trade-offs and verify that the explanation is not memorized marketing.

concepts.boundary: A focused unit test does not prove Compose, PostgreSQL, provider, browser, or public behavior unless those boundaries are exercised.
concepts.narration: For each claim, name one exact source seam and one behavior test. Explain what the test would catch and which runtime boundaries it does not cross.
concepts.scenario: A candidate cites a class declaration as proof that the feature is used by chat.
options: Trace the route and factory usage before claiming wiring
concepts.scenario_explanation: Code existence and live-path wiring are separate dimensions.

concepts.label: Demo Proof Path
concepts.summary: A short demo shows one run, one governed effect, evidence, evaluation, and explicit limits with synthetic data.

teaching.definition: The demo proof path is a rehearsed sequence of observable product behavior backed by a revision-scoped fallback artifact.
receives: Ready local stack or recorded evidence
teaching.responsibility: Show answer, ordered events, policy/approval, tool result, evidence, and evaluation without exposing credentials or inventing live success.
controls: No env, token, key, or raw credential display
teaching.failure_behavior: If Docker or a provider fails, switch to clearly labeled recorded evidence rather than simulating a completed command.
teaching.why_it_matters: A demo should prove system behavior under time pressure while preserving the same evidence standards as engineering work.

concepts.boundary: Recorded evidence proves its recorded revision and environment, not the current runtime unless revalidated.
concepts.narration: The demo path is intentionally narrow: inspect one run, show one exact approval and effect, then connect evidence to evaluation. Use synthetic data and a predeclared recorded-evidence fallback.
concepts.scenario: The live provider is unavailable thirty seconds before the demo.
options: Use recorded revision-scoped evidence and label it
concepts.scenario_explanation: The fallback preserves truth and timing without pretending live execution.

concepts.label: Trade-offs
concepts.summary: Strong answers explain why explicit contracts improve auditability while adding persistence and coordination cost.

teaching.definition: A trade-off states the benefit purchased by a design and the cost, complexity, or limitation accepted in return.
teaching.responsibility: Explain why custom typed control, durable approvals, SQL-JSON retrieval, or local Compose fit this capstone without declaring them universally best.
controls: Cost and operational burden remain visible
teaching.failure_behavior: Feature-only answers sound shallow; claiming one design is always superior ignores context and undermines senior-level judgment.
teaching.why_it_matters: Interviewers use trade-offs to distinguish implementation familiarity from architecture reasoning.

concepts.boundary: Current choices optimize inspectability and reproducibility, not global scale, lowest latency, or least code.
concepts.narration: Name both sides of each decision. The custom runtime makes authority and failures explicit but costs more engineering. SQL-JSON retrieval is portable and inspectable but not a high-scale vector index.
concepts.scenario: Why not use an agent framework?
options: Explicit contracts were central here, but a matching framework could reduce cost
concepts.scenario_explanation: The decision is contextual, not ideological.

concepts.label: Failure Story
concepts.summary: A strong STAR story shows diagnosis, root-cause correction, regression coverage, and rerun evidence.

teaching.definition: A failure story is a concise situation-task-action-result narrative grounded in a real defect that crossed a boundary static checks missed.
teaching.responsibility: Explain how evidence narrowed the fault, why the fix addressed the class, and what new test prevents recurrence.
controls: Symptoms are separated from root cause
teaching.failure_behavior: If the story ends at a code edit without rerunning the real boundary, it proves activity rather than resolution.
teaching.why_it_matters: Real failures reveal engineering method, evidence discipline, and the ability to learn from deployment boundaries.

concepts.boundary: One fixed incident does not establish general reliability or eliminate related risks.
concepts.narration: Use a real failure story: reproduce, inspect evidence, fix the root boundary, add regression coverage, and rerun the affected acceptance. State what the result still does not prove.
concepts.scenario: A DR seed fails because PostgreSQL rejects a NUL-containing advisory-lock key.
options: Fix canonical key serialization, add a regression, and rerun clean restore
concepts.scenario_explanation: The documented story fixes the production data boundary and re-exercises recovery.

concepts.label: Security Boundary Answer
concepts.summary: Security explanations trace untrusted input through validation, policy, exact approval, isolated execution, redaction, and scoped persistence.

teaching.definition: A security boundary answer identifies the asset, untrusted input, deterministic control, fail-closed behavior, and residual trusted infrastructure.
teaching.responsibility: Explain how model, user, document, MCP, and tool data are constrained without claiming absolute security.
controls: Secrets and hidden reasoning are excluded from evidence
teaching.failure_behavior: Unknown or mismatched effects fail closed; host compromise and operator error remain outside application guarantees.
teaching.why_it_matters: Security credibility comes from explicit trust boundaries and failure behavior, not from adjectives such as secure or enterprise-grade.

concepts.boundary: No independent security audit, hostile multi-tenant certification, or public-edge threat model is claimed.
concepts.narration: Security answers should name the untrusted input, deterministic control, fail-closed outcome, and residual trusted boundary. The local Docker daemon, host, env file, and keys remain trusted.
concepts.scenario: An interviewer asks whether the sandbox makes arbitrary code completely safe.
options: Describe networkless container controls and the lack of VM-grade certification
concepts.scenario_explanation: The answer presents both containment evidence and residual boundary.

concepts.label: Operations Answer
concepts.summary: Operational credibility separates recipes, CI, local readiness, recovery observations, and absent public SLOs.

teaching.definition: An operations answer explains how one revision is built, migrated, started, probed, observed, backed up, restored, and bounded by its environment.
receives: Health, readiness, telemetry, and recovery evidence
teaching.responsibility: Distinguish verification pipelines from deployment and measurements from adopted objectives.
controls: Only the managed wrapper operates retained state
Checksums and clean-target guards protect restore
teaching.failure_behavior: A failed readiness or restore blocks the claim; a timeout, manifest, or old log is never substituted for current evidence.
teaching.why_it_matters: Operations is where code presence becomes an exercised service boundary and where overclaiming is easiest to detect.

concepts.boundary: No public ingress, managed cloud database, hosted telemetry, on-call, load test, or adopted production RTO/RPO exists.
concepts.narration: Operations evidence is layered: CI verifies a revision, readiness observes a local target, and recovery measures one drill. None is public deployment or an adopted production SLO.
concepts.scenario: A candidate quotes one local restore time as the product RTO.
options: Call it one observed restore-to-ready measurement, not an objective
concepts.scenario_explanation: An observation is not an approved business objective.

concepts.label: Honest Close
concepts.summary: Close with the strongest proven capability, the biggest trade-off, and explicit deferred boundaries.

teaching.definition: The honest close summarizes what the repository demonstrates, why the design matters, and what evidence would be required for the next claim.
teaching.responsibility: Finish with confidence proportional to evidence and invite follow-up at exact source or failure boundaries.
controls: Deferred does not imply promised delivery
teaching.failure_behavior: A close that says production-ready, infinitely scalable, or fully secure contradicts the evidence and damages the entire presentation.
teaching.why_it_matters: Senior communication includes negative space: knowing what was deliberately not built and why.

concepts.boundary: Distributed swarms, GPU serving, training, public deployment, anonymous sharing, autonomous mutation, and adopted cloud recovery objectives remain deferred or absent.
concepts.narration: Close by naming the strongest proof and the negative space. Archon demonstrates an evidence-rich local control plane; public deployment, production scale, training, and autonomous mutation remain outside the claim.
concepts.scenario: The interviewer asks what remains incomplete.
options: Name public operations, scale, provider breadth, and deferred capabilities with evidence requirements
concepts.scenario_explanation: Explicit gaps demonstrate judgment and preserve the capstone's credibility.
